clue.text: "There's no doubt in my mind that -'s won, but I'm not sure just what" (Ken Kesey)

definitions.text: "There's no doubt in my mind that -'s won, but I'm not sure just what" (Ken Kesey)

parts.words: "There's no doubt in my mind that -'s won, but I'm not sure just what" (Ken Kesey)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing name is the hero of Kesey's novel One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, the rebel patient who takes on Nurse Ratched

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue: the gap is filled by the surname of Kesey's own protagonist, Randle Patrick, the brawling patient of the Oregon asylum ward.
explanation.definitionFit: Kesey's line is about the outcome for his own hero, the patient Randle Patrick of Cuckoo's Nest, so the blank takes that character's surname.

clue.text: Red fog shrouding outskirts of Acapulco

indicators.note: to shroud is to wrap or cover, so the fog surrounds the letters inside it

parts.note: mist is a thin fog

indicators.note: the outskirts are the edges, so the first and last letters of the city name

explanation.surface: A red fog hangs over the edge of a Mexican resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red' looks like a colour, but it is the political sense: a communist.
explanation.definitionFit: Red is a common term for a communist, and a follower of Chairman Mao is one.

clue.text: Tamil tongue extract for Secretary for Foreign Tongues

indicators.note: an extract is a passage taken from inside a longer text, so the letters run inside these words

explanation.surface: A passage of Tamil is given to the government official responsible for foreign languages.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet of Paradise Lost served Cromwell's government as Secretary for Foreign Tongues, writing its Latin letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet of Paradise Lost was appointed Secretary for Foreign Tongues by Cromwell's Council of State in 1649.

clue.text: Brave trio messing around Walter Scott, perhaps

indicators.note: messing around suggests disorder, so the letters are shuffled into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Three brave men fooling about with Walter Scott.
explanation.walkthrough: Not the novelist: several Mississippi steamboats were named Walter Scott, one of which Twain mentions in Huckleberry Finn.
explanation.definitionFit: The wrecked steamboat Walter Scott in Huckleberry Finn is a paddle steamer, a vessel built for river work.

clue.text: Rudkus's prison protest urges thinker to change

indicators.note: to change means the letters are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: A prisoner's protest urges a philosopher to change their mind.
explanation.walkthrough: Jurgis Rudkus is the immigrant hero of Upton Sinclair's The Jungle, a novel of starvation wages, so refusing food is apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Refusing all food is a classic form of protest by prisoners, here linked to the starving hero of The Jungle.

clue.text: Banville novel recalling Hungary in a European group

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so the assembled letters are taken back the other way
Hungary sits inside the word for a group

parts.note: a set is a group of things belonging together
H is the international vehicle code for Hungary

explanation.surface: A Banville novel that harks back to Hungary's place in some European bloc.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts H inside SET to make SEHT; A, E and that SEHT give AESEHT, and 'recalling' turns the lot round to the title.
explanation.definitionFit: John Banville's Booker-winning 2005 book is titled after the coast where its narrator spent childhood holidays.

clue.text: Greek travel writer in Russia at the front

parts.note: someone who is in is at home

indicators.note: only the leading letter of the word Russia is taken

explanation.surface: A Greek travel writer on assignment with the army in Russia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a link but supplies HOME, as in 'stay in'. The Odyssey, a tale of ten years' wandering, makes its poet a jokey travel writer.
explanation.definitionFit: The epic poet of the Odyssey chronicled Odysseus's long voyage home, so he is playfully cast as a travel writer.

clue.text: Writer and social reformer wrong about beastly housing

parts.note: a sin is a wrong, a moral offence
C stands for circa, Latin for about
a lair is the den where a wild beast lives

explanation.surface: A campaigning writer is criticised for misjudging the state of animal accommodation.
explanation.definitionFit: Upton Sinclair exposed the meatpacking industry in The Jungle and campaigned for socialist causes, so he was both novelist and reformer.

clue.text: Dope upset leader gets on makes things a bit better

parts.note: a dope is a fool, an ass

indicators.note: the leader of the next word is its opening letter only

parts.note: to get on is to grow older, to age

explanation.surface: A dazed addict upsets the ringleader, who then ages but improves things slightly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' is not an anagram signal here: 'leader' takes its first letter, U.
explanation.definitionFit: To assuage is to ease or soothe, which leaves a bad situation somewhat improved.

clue.text: Look over literature about camper English novelist

indicators.note: over signals that the short word for look is turned the other way

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or behold

indicators.note: the word for literature wraps round the word for a camper

parts.note: a camper is a camper van, a van fitted out for living in

explanation.surface: Reviewing books on the camping life of an English author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'camper' looks like a person in a tent, but it is the camper van. Alfred Ollivant is little read now; he wrote the sheepdog novel Owd Bob.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Ollivant was an English writer of fiction, best known for the sheepdog story Owd Bob of 1898.

clue.text: Manuscript author primarily reflects, finishes and revises

indicators.note: a mirror reflection turns the picked letters round so they read backwards
primarily means take the first letter of each of the two words

parts.note: ends are finishes, conclusions

explanation.surface: An author goes over a manuscript, ponders, completes it and makes corrections.
explanation.walkthrough: 'primarily' takes M and A from Manuscript and author; 'reflects' turns MA into AM.
explanation.definitionFit: To amend a text is to correct or alter it, which is what revising it does.

clue.text: A curt seminar breaking down Meyer novel

indicators.note: breaking down suggests the phrase is taken apart and the letters rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: A short, sharp seminar on dismantling a Meyer book.
explanation.walkthrough: Philipp Meyer, not Twilight's Stephenie Meyer, is the author: his 2009 debut is about a Pennsylvania steel town in decline.
explanation.definitionFit: Philipp Meyer's first novel, of 2009, follows two young men in a declining Pennsylvania steel valley.

clue.text: Kent banker's revolutionary books written in Russia

indicators.note: a revolution turns things round, so the assembled letters are read backwards
the books are set down inside the abbreviation for Russia

parts.note: RUS is the international abbreviation for Russia
OT is the Old Testament, the first books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A Kent bank manager's subversive literature, composed in Russia.
explanation.walkthrough: The Stour is a river in Kent, and a river has banks, so in crossword language it is a 'banker'.
explanation.definitionFit: A banker in crosswords can be a river, which has banks; the Great Stour flows through Canterbury in Kent.

clue.text: Dancer gypsies raised seen with Stone around southern area

indicators.note: the gemstone goes round the letter for southern

parts.note: an emerald is a precious green stone

explanation.surface: A dancing woman from a family of travellers is seen alongside a rock in a southern region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gypsies raised' looks like a reversal signal but belongs to the definition: Hugo's dancer was brought up by gypsies. 'around' puts EMERALD round S.
explanation.definitionFit: In Victor Hugo's Notre-Dame de Paris the heroine is a street dancer brought up by gypsies.

clue.text: "The radical of one century is the of the next." (Mark Twain)

definitions.text: "The radical of one century is the of the next." (Mark Twain)

parts.words: "The radical of one century is the of the next." (Mark Twain)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing word is the opposite of a radical, the person who wants things kept as they are

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue: Twain's point is that yesterday's radical idea becomes the next age's establishment view.
explanation.definitionFit: Twain sets the radical against its opposite, the traditionalist who resists change, so the gap takes that word.

clue.text: German actor pursuing very tired crime queen

indicators.note: pursuing means following behind, so the German actor comes after the words for very tired

parts.note: all in means exhausted, very tired
a ham is an overacting actor

explanation.surface: A German actor chases an exhausted female crime boss.
explanation.walkthrough: Margery Allingham, creator of Albert Campion, was one of the four 'Queens of Crime' of the golden age of detective fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: Margery Allingham, Campion's creator, was ranked with Christie, Sayers and Marsh as a Queen of Crime of golden-age detective fiction.

clue.text: Small fridge for Maria Stuart designer

parts.note: a chiller is a refrigerator, a cold cabinet

explanation.surface: A compact refrigerator for a fashion designer called Maria Stuart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'designer' sounds like fashion, but here it means the playwright who designed the drama Maria Stuart, Friedrich Schiller.
explanation.definitionFit: Friedrich Schiller wrote the 1800 tragedy Maria Stuart, so he was the play's creator or designer.

clue.text: On film, performer is Edmund Pevensie, say

indicators.note: on places the performer on top of, so before, the word for a film

parts.note: a turn is a performer in a variety show
a coat is a thin film or layer

explanation.surface: In a film adaptation, an actor plays Edmund Pevensie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On film' suggests cinema, but 'film' is a thin layer, COAT. In Lewis's Narnia, Edmund betrays his siblings to the White Witch.
explanation.definitionFit: Edmund Pevensie betrays his brother and sisters to the White Witch in Lewis's Narnia, making him a traitor to his side.

clue.text: I want no stake in company a French ultra and cad ruined

parts.note: un is the French word for a

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked, so these letters are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: An investor refuses shares in a firm wrecked by a French extremist and a scoundrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I want no stake in company' reads as a shareholder's refusal, but 'I want no stake' is the vampire, dreading a wooden stake through the heart.
explanation.definitionFit: Stoker's vampire Count is destroyed by a wooden stake through the heart, so he would want none.

clue.text: Old and popular creative work about Lucentio's man

indicators.note: about here means turned around, so the whole assembled run is read backwards

parts.note: in means popular, fashionable
art is creative work

explanation.surface: Old, popular art concerning a Shakespearean servant.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Taming of the Shrew, Lucentio's servant swaps places with his master to help his courtship.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Taming of the Shrew, Lucentio's servant Tranio poses as his master while Lucentio woos Bianca.

clue.text: Boat base found around new northern home of Nana?

indicators.note: the boat base is placed around the two single letters

parts.note: the keel is the structural spine along the bottom of a boat

explanation.surface: A boat's base is discovered near a new northern home for Grandma.
explanation.walkthrough: Nana is the Newfoundland dog who acts as nursemaid to the Darling children in Peter Pan; she sleeps in a doghouse in the garden.
explanation.definitionFit: Nana, the Darling family's Newfoundland in Peter Pan, sleeps in a doghouse, the usual shelter for a dog.

clue.text: One article published by family for Fox producer

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
an is the indefinite article
a newspaper ran a story when it published it
kin are one's family

explanation.surface: One family-published piece is credited to a Fox television producer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fox' is not the TV network: Malcolm Fox is a detective in the novels of the Scottish crime writer Ian Rankin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish crime writer created Inspector Malcolm Fox of the Complaints department, so he is the character's maker.

clue.text: Losing weight, varies in states

indicators.note: losing means the letter for weight drops out of the word

parts.note: something that wavers varies or fluctuates
W is the physics symbol for weight

explanation.surface: Someone dieting finds their weight fluctuates in different states.
explanation.walkthrough: 'states' is a verb here, meaning declares, not countries.
explanation.definitionFit: To aver is to declare or assert firmly, a synonym of stating.

clue.text: New moneybag, take penny out for Tribulation Periwinkle?

indicators.note: take, with out later, signals removing the letter for penny
out completes take out, the instruction to remove the penny letter

parts.note: a purse is a small bag for money

explanation.surface: A newly rich person's money bag has a penny removed.
explanation.walkthrough: Tribulation Periwinkle is the pen-name and heroine of Louisa May Alcott's Hospital Sketches, about tending Civil War wounded.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcott's Tribulation Periwinkle tends wounded soldiers in a Civil War hospital, based on Alcott's own wartime ward work.

clue.text: Large literary prize ignoring the book Helen of Troy?

indicators.note: ignoring means leaving out the letter for book

parts.note: the Booker is a leading British literary prize
B is the abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: A major book award that takes no notice of an epic about Helen of Troy.
explanation.walkthrough: The Booker Prize is Britain's best-known fiction award. Helen of Troy, 'the face that launched a thousand ships', is the example of a beauty.
explanation.definitionFit: Helen of Troy is the classic example of a stunningly attractive woman, the sort called a stunner.

clue.text: Daisy, perhaps, in a bunch arranged by a knight

indicators.note: flowers arranged are rearranged, so the letters of these words are put in a new order

parts.note: N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: A daisy among a bunch of flowers arranged by a knight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daisy' looks like the flower, but it is Daisy, the heroine of Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby, whose married surname this is.
explanation.definitionFit: Daisy, Gatsby's lost love in Fitzgerald's novel, is married to Tom, so she carries his surname.

clue.text: Have another screening of Alien in breaktime?

indicators.note: the alien is put inside the word for a break

parts.note: a rest is a break
ET is the alien of Spielberg's film E.T.

explanation.surface: Showing the film Alien again during an interval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'screening' suggests cinema, as does 'Alien', but here it is a medical screening, done a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: To screen is to test for disease, so a repeat screening is a second test.

clue.text: Destination of Greene's train and boat: slum needing repair

indicators.note: something needing repair is broken, so the letters are rearranged into new order

explanation.surface: Where Greene's train and a boat end up: a run-down district.
explanation.walkthrough: Graham Greene's 1932 novel Stamboul Train runs on the Orient Express to Istanbul, then called by this old name.
explanation.definitionFit: Greene's Stamboul Train takes its name from its terminus, the old European name for Istanbul.
